answers.answer: No helper takes an argument; you type each one exactly as shown. For progress use {charity.name}, {charity.raised}, {charity.target}, {charity.percent} or {charity.bar}, plus {charity.link} for the website. For donations use {charity.donations.count} and {charity.donations.latest}. The page gives a ready reply that combines progress and the newest donation.
answers.quote: None of these helpers takes an input, so type each one exactly as shown.

answers.answer: You need to know how braces work in a reply; the first paragraph sends you to Variables and templates if you do not. The bot also needs the Twitch permission channel:read:charity, which your first sign-in does not ask for. You grant it from Settings, then Integrations, while signed in to Twitch as the streamer's own account. A campaign must be running on Twitch.
answers.quote: To read your campaign, the bot needs your Twitch permission channel:read:charity.

answers.answer: Success is a reply that shows values, such as the example output with the name, the amounts, the bar and the donor. Failure is a helper printed with its braces. The cause table tells the three causes apart: a missing permission, no running campaign, or Twitch not answering. After the grant, the notice title reads Permissions granted.
answers.quote: When a helper has nothing to show, it prints exactly as you typed it, braces and all.

answers.answer: Use {charity.name}: {charity.raised} of {charity.target} {charity.bar}. Thank you, {charity.donations.latest}! With no active campaign, the progress helpers print as typed, so use the command only on charity streams and switch it off otherwise. Before the first donation, {charity.donations.latest} prints as typed, so leave out the thank-you until then.
answers.quote: With no campaign running, {charity.name}, {charity.raised}, {charity.target} and {charity.bar} print as typed, so use the command only on your charity streams.

answers.answer: I reread one passage. The page asks me to type my charity command in chat to check the permission before it shows any charity command; the command example only comes in the last section. That costs a jump forward, but the reader already knows how to make a command, so no step is missing.
answers.quote: So type your charity command once in your channel’s chat before a charity stream, and then look at Needs attention.

answers.answer: Nothing confusing is left. Read aloud, the block characters of the bar cannot be voiced, but the page then spells the bar out in words, so a listener can follow it.
answers.quote: In words, the example bar is four filled blocks, then six pale blocks, then 42%.

warning_review.reason: Five short sentences, each one a separate fact the reader needs to grant the permission: who sees the Grant permissions button, which Twitch account must approve the code, and that the streamer's own account is the one to use. The count is not hiding a step, and each sentence is one the reader can act on.

Five short sentences of formatting facts: the currency symbol and decimals, the digit grouping and where the language is set, the English default, and the currency-code fallback. The reader can find the one they need, and the Language pointer is useful. No sentence is a defect for a streamer who is writing a reply.
